brief.situation: 14:00 in an outpatient neurologic clinic. You are the physical therapist assistant, carrying out the physical therapist's plan. Mrs. Arslan, 58, is on visit 4 for right vestibular hypofunction. She says the dizziness had been improving, but since lunch she 'sees double' when she looks to the left.
handover: Plan of care (Dr. Klein, PT): gaze stabilization (head turns while fixing on a target), static and dynamic balance progression, home program 3 times a day. Hypertension and diabetes.

Clinic policy: stop and report any new neurological symptom (double vision, slurred speech, facial droop, limb weakness or clumsiness, a new severe headache) to the PT at once; the PT reexamines and calls 911 if a stroke is suspected, noting the time last known well.
Dr. Klein is in the gym next door.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time at the pace you choose: study pace (3x) or exam realism (1x). Pause any time.
Each question or measure takes the time on its button. Decide what to collect, what it means for today's session and who needs to know.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

why.question: Mrs. Arslan has new double vision, slurred speech and a clumsy left hand. What does this mean for the session, and who decides?

parts.label: What the data show
parts.criteria: New double vision, slurred speech and limb clumsiness are central signs, not peripheral vestibular symptoms; with hypertension and diabetes they could be a stroke; the vestibular plan may not apply to central disorders.
parts.modelAnswer: Double vision, slurred speech and a clumsy hand are new neurological signs, not part of her vestibular hypofunction. With her blood pressure and diabetes, this could be a stroke.

parts.label: What I do and who decides
parts.criteria: Stops and seats her; notes last known well; tells the PT now with the data; the PT reexamines and calls 911; documents data.
parts.modelAnswer: I stop and sit her down, note 12:30 as last known well, and get Dr. Klein now. She reexamines and decides about 911; I document the data and times.

scoring.modelReasoning: Gaze stabilization is meant to provoke some dizziness in peripheral hypofunction, but double vision, slurred speech and limb clumsiness are new central signs. The PTA stops, seats her, notes the time last known well and tells the supervising PT at once with the data. The PT reexamines and calls 911; the note records data, not a diagnosis.
